transcript: Solution engineer: What is the problem you are trying to solve?
Nursing director: Nurses spend the start of every shift hunting for infusion pumps. We own plenty, we just cannot find them.
Biomedical engineering lead: We have about four hundred pumps across the main building. Roughly a hundred are in maintenance or missing at any time.
Finance partner: We bought sixty more last year and the shortage did not change. That is the number I care about.
Solution engineer: Is there any tagging on the pumps today?
Biomedical engineering lead: They all have BLE tags. We fitted them two years ago for a project that never went live.
IT security lead: About half of them have tags. The rest were never fitted because the vendor ran out and nobody followed up.
Biomedical engineering lead: That does not match my records, but I will check.
Solution engineer: What would you want to see?
Nursing director: Where the nearest available pump is, on the ward, from a phone. That is it.
Biomedical engineering lead: And a flag when a pump has not moved for more than a day, because that usually means it is in a cupboard.
Solution engineer: Which wards for a pilot?
Nursing director: Two medical wards on the third floor. They are the worst for it.
IT security lead: Anything that tracks a device near a patient goes through our privacy review. The tags do not carry patient data, but the location history could imply it.
Solution engineer: What does that review need?
IT security lead: A data flow, a retention period and a named owner. It takes about a month.
Finance partner: How will we know it worked?
Nursing director: Time to find a pump. Ask any nurse and they will say twenty minutes, but nobody has timed it.
Solution engineer: Would you be willing to time it for a week before the pilot?
Nursing director: Yes, if someone gives the ward a simple sheet.
Biomedical engineering lead: The gateways for BLE are already on the ceilings on the third floor. I cannot say whether they are all powered.
IT security lead: They are on the building network, which is fine. No cloud for the location data without the review.
Solution engineer: Understood. Who would own the pilot day to day?
Nursing director: One of my ward managers, once I pick one.
Finance partner: We also talked about tracking wheelchairs. Not now.
Solution engineer: I will note it as discussed, not in scope.
Biomedical engineering lead: One thing. Some pumps go to the sterilisation unit in the basement and the tags do not work through those walls. Do not count those as missing.
Solution engineer: Good to know. Anything else before I draft?
IT security lead: Just that the review starts when the data flow exists, so send that first.

requirements.note: from a phone on the ward

traps.note: All pumps have BLE tags (L6) versus about half (L7).
The pilot owner has not been named.
Retention period is required by the privacy review and was not stated.

follow_up.real_answer: The nursing director has named the ward manager of the third floor east ward as the day-to-day pilot owner.
follow_up.non_answer: Still deciding, will get back to you.
